worth_building: R4 (SSD-tier order through file times), in the form the replay supports, not the draft's: touch the pages a lookup finds (or refresh a session's chain once per request or per 300 s), put an ended session's pages past its first prompt first, and re-check a file's time before the unlink. At campaign 34's setting the cleaner starts at minute 88 and costs 0.72-0.93 M tokens of recompute per 20 minutes (1.01-1.28 M from the first pass to 6,600 s). That is 1.3-1.7 s of mean TTFT in minutes 90-110 at the measured weight N - B = 108 (1.7-2.0 s at N = 128 as the analyst computed; mean there 27-28 s) and about 0.3 s of the 110-minute mean of 10.7-11.5 s. Touch on read or refresh alone leaves 0.07-0.08 s, with the tail rule 0.02-0.04 s (my replay, three arms). It is the only candidate whose gain is above the 0.8 s by which arms differ in a window for no measured reason. The TTFT figure is inferred through the closed-loop identity; a minute regression inside campaign 34 finds about half the predicted loss of throughput, so a GPU run is needed for the size.

F5 (a lookup that finds nothing is free, and no lookup for text no tier holds): small and cheap. History lost by turns left with no lookup: 59 K tokens (ec_full), 303 K (jit_exact), 23 K (ec_exact), 592 K (jit_p50), which is about 0.02, 0.09, 0.01 and 0.16 s per request at the weight of the minutes it falls in. Direct part: a turn with an empty lookup waits a median 16 ms longer and 29-31 % of returning turns have one at light load, about 5 ms per returning turn (1-11 ms by means). For the hicache baseline the allowance is 53.6 M tokens, 81 % of its lost history, but that arm runs as is by the author's decision.

PR1 (measure and log the prices), as instrumentation with the definitions changed; no TTFT gain by itself. mu should be users in session minus running requests (108 at saturation; measured 93-94 over minutes 90-110 and 99-101 in the last ten), not 1 + ready turns (30.6). c as 'no other ready turn' is 0.85-0.94 until minute 28, 0.05 in minutes 28-70 and 0 after, but before the user cap binds it understates the weight of stall (0.35-0.46 from jit_p50). kappa is 0 as a price where late reads exist. The marginal-holder lambda is about 2e-7 at light load against the fixed 5e-5. Recompute cost on FA3 is 0.012 ms per token plus 1.46 us per token per K of position, not Triton's 0.11 ms and not constant in the context length.

End signal fix, a precondition for R1 and R4 rather than a listed candidate: 'no table entry for the reply key' must not register a session as ended. 411 commits per run are falsely ended in the table-hint arms; their next requests read from the SSD 89-92 % of the time after pauses under 10 s against 5-19 % for others (3.3 M tokens, 6 % of ec_full's reads in minutes 30-110). The direct TTFT footprint is small, about 0.02 s of ec_full's mean.
not_worth_building: F1 (landing quantile for the hold): no measurable gain. The hold fires almost only with the pool at 0.90 or more (2 of 2,873 holds below), where c is 0.06 or less. Held reads are 5.6 % of turns; their own stall is 0.14-0.16 s per held read in minutes 30-70 and 0.8-1.4 s in 70-90. Going from a 2 s to a 4 s margin removes 0.27 s per held read, about 0.016 s per request at weight 1 and less at the measured weights, for 38 K more token-seconds pinned per held read. The memory side is about 1 % of the host pool (14.7 K tokens on average in minutes 30-70). With c measured where the hold binds the quantile goes to 1 and lands held reads late on purpose.

F2 (c in the expected-cost start): nothing to gain at this setting. The arm already stages 1 read, and the most a read before arrival could save is 0.000-0.016 s per returning request in minutes 0-30, 0.002 s c-weighted in 30-70 and 0 after. It is needed only as a guard if F3 is built, and its c must not be the ready-queue c before the user cap binds.

F3 (read time that counts the line before arrival), alone: harmful. With the true read time and stall weight 1 the rule would stage reads for 53 % of the stalled readers of minutes 70-110 (638 of 1,207; 61 % at 2e-5) into a read thread that is 100 % busy, which is what cost jit_p50 its 0.7-1.3 s. With F2 it stages none, so the pair gains nothing here. The calibration worth doing instead is the lag seed: 0.9 s in the engine against 0.05 s measured.

F4 (read-or-recompute by price at light load): 57-78 readers arrive to an idle GPU in 40 minutes (1.0-1.4 % of returning requests). Recomputing saves each 0.29-0.33 s but 1.5-1.7 turns arrive during it and lose 0.6-0.9 s, so recomputing every idle arrival nets -34 and -12 TTFT-seconds (ec_full, jit_p50); the own saving alone is +0.003 s per returning request. With exact hints there is almost nothing to act on (4-5 such readers).

R1 as written (skip an ended session's last write and mark its chain first out): the skip saves 1.49 M tokens (4.7 % of writes), under 1 % of the device at saturation, and only 0.23 M if the end is known at the reply. Marking the whole chain first out is worse than today (3.3-4.0 s against 1.7-2.0 s by N g). Only the pages past the first prompt may go first, which belongs to R4, and today's end signal is wrong 411 times a run.

R2 (write queue in eviction order): no gain at this setting. Writes are acked a median 0.5-0.7 s after submit (p90 1.7-2.1 s), no host eviction came back short, and pending writes hold a p90 of 13-15 K tokens. It is a stability lever of campaign 32's kind (27 against 6 ops pending, oldest 5.8 against 0.9 s), which only a GPU run with merging off could show.
R3 (clean only on a full acknowledgement): no test in these runs. No write failed (0 failed groups) and no op stayed unacked in campaign 34.

R5 (restore-cost-aware order, only copies stay): nothing to gain at this setting. Before the cleaner starts the best arms lose 4-25 K tokens of history in 88 minutes (7-10 requests); after it the loss is the SSD tier's, which R4 covers.
P1 (staged reads yield before queued turns, queued turns by slack): no evidence. Campaign 34 has no refused read before the deadline, no bump, and 1 to 39 staged reads in the expected-cost arms.

P2 (reads against writes by due date and clean reserve): no TTFT gain at this setting. The 27-30 holds per run cost 8-14 s of read-thread time in two hours, and 22-24 of them fired on one cold prompt of 50 K+ tokens whose request was still running, memory eviction could not take anyway. The 50 K threshold measures the wrong thing; the replacement is unproven as a stability lever without a GPU run.
cautions: The analysts' numbers hold up: of about 30 groups of claims rechecked with my own parsers, queue rebuild and page-level replay, all but three reproduce, most to the printed digit. The three: the 60 % 'every earlier holder was already over' (31 %, 66 % or 84 % depending on who counts as a holder), the 79-98 % of long-pause requests that read in minutes 0-70 (16-83 % by my count), and ev_write's split of the cleaner's cost, whose parts sum above the cleaner-attributable total. None changes a build decision.

The R4 gain is a token count converted by an identity, not an observed TTFT change. ev_ssd converts at N = 128; the measured weight is N - B = 108 (93-94 over minutes 90-110), which lowers 1.6-1.9 s to 1.3-1.7 s. Inside campaign 34 the per-minute loss of admissions per K tokens recomputed is -0.042 +- 0.025 against -0.093 predicted, so the gain could be half of that.

Stall is not free before the user cap binds. In minutes 60-85 jit_p50's extra 5.5 s of reader stall per request cost +1.7 to +1.9 s on the same requests with no difference in recompute, through 2 % more requests served, a shorter mean pause per request and 2-3 more users in session; after the cap the difference is 0.4-0.6 s and not distinguishable from 0. So section 7.8 holds only after the cap, and a c read off the ready queue (0.05 in minutes 28-70) would understate the weight there. One run per arm.

Selection in the hint evidence: the falling hazard is a property of the FreeInference trees that pass the 65,536-token filter, at x1. Campaign 26's gaps are near-deterministic (tool gaps 6.8-7.4 s at x10, p90/p10 median 3.7 on the entries sent), so the draft's section 3.3 sentence that explains campaign 26 by falling hazards is wrong, and campaign 26's exact-hint gain was measured where a table median is almost exact.

Clock definition: a cleaner pass's logged time is its end; the scan starts 10-12 s earlier and the unlinks come in its last second. 'Before the first pass' cut at the logged time includes 2-5 requests that lost history to that pass (62-159 K tokens); cut at the scan's start the loss is 4-25 K.

Double counting: ev_write's 1.05-1.19 M plus 0.23-0.24 M for the cleaner exceeds the cleaner-attributable loss (1.01-1.23 M per arm, first requests 129-143 K of it); ev_ssd (1.21 M) and ev_prices (1.19 M) agree with my 1.23 M for ec_full.

Counterfactuals that hold something fixed: every SSD order is replayed on the recorded timeline and lookups; a replay that leaves out the rewrite after a loss overstates the whole-chain order fourfold. The margin replay keeps the read line as it was. The 'F3 alone' count keeps each reader's measured stall, while 600 more early reads would lengthen the line. The oracle-write saving keeps evictions as they were.

Draft constants to correct: section 2's read lags are 0.05 s, not 0.9 s; recompute cost rises with position, so 'recompute always wins on an idle GPU' fails past about 45 K tokens; section 4.3's 'ended sessions' chains first' is harmful as written; section 6's mu formula gives 30.6 where the measured weight is 93-108.

Not established here: the run-to-run spread in the saturated phase (arms differ by up to 0.8 s in a window without differing in stall), the closed-loop effect of any SSD order, the cost of the file touches on this volume, the page-exit times behind ev_write's write due dates, campaign 32's chain bound under pending writes, ev_ssd's three-class and index orders, and campaign 26's ceiling.
